la:verb:mitto.html:
mitto, mīsi, missum, 3 (contr. form, misti for misisti, : archaic
inf. pass. mittier, ), v. a.
etym. dub.; cf. Sanscr. math-, to set in motion
, to cause to go, let go, send, to send off, despatch, etc.
In gen.: ad Trojam cum misi ob defendendam Graeciam, Enn. ap. (Trag. v. 362 Vahl.): filium suum foras ad propinquum suum quendam mittit,: signa ... quam plurima quam primumque mittas,: legatos de deditione ad eum miserunt,: pabulatum mittebat,: scitatum oracula,: Delphos consultum,: missus sum, te ut requirerem,: ego huc missa sum ludere,: equitatum auxilio Caesari Aedui miserant,: alicui subsidium,: ad subsidium,: misi, pro amicitiā, qui hoc diceret,: qui solveret,: mittite ambo hominem,.—With acc. and inf.: Deiotarus legatos ad me misit, se cum omnibus copiis esse venturum,sent me word that,: ad collegam mittit, opus esse exercitu,: Publilius duo milia militum recepta miserat,: Dexagoridas miserat ad legatum Romanum traditurum se urbem,: statim Athenas mittit se cum exercitu venturum,. Missum facere is also used for mittere, to send: ut cohortis ad me missum facias, Pompei. ap.

, B, 2: aliquem morti,to put to death, despatch,; so, ad mortem,: in possessionem,to put in possession,: aliquem ad cenam,to invite one to dinner,: sub jugum mittere, to send or cause to go under the yoke, : sub jugo,—

In partic.
To send word, announce, tell, report any thing to any one: ut mihi vadimonia dilata et Chresti conpilationem mitteres,: Curio misi, ut medico honos haberetur,: mitti ad principes placuit, ut secernerent se ab Etruscis,: hodie Spintherem exspecto: misit enim Brutus ad me,: salutem alicui,to send greeting to, to greet one,: ita existimes velim, me antelaturum fuisse, si ad me misisses, voluntatem tuam commodo meo,i. e. if you had sent to me for aid, applied to me,.—
To send as a compliment, to dedicate to any one, of a book or poem: liber Antiochi, qui ab eo ad Balbum missus est,: hunc librum de Senectute ad te misimus,.—
To send, yield, produce, furnish, export any thing (as the product of a country): India mittit ebur, molles sua tura Sabaei,: (Padus) electra nuribus mittit gestanda Latinis,; cf.: quos frigida misit Nursia,: hordea, quae Libyci ratibus misere coloni,: quas mittit dives Panchaia merces,; ; .—
To dismiss a thing from the mind: maestumque timorem Mittite,: mittere ac finire odium,: leves spes,: missam iram facere,.—
To put an end to, end: certamen,.—
Esp. in speaking, etc., to pass over, omit, to give over, cease, forbear (cf.: praetermitto, praetereo, relinquo): quin tu istas mittis tricas?: mitto proelia, praetereo oppugnationes oppidorum,omit,: maledicta omnia,.—With inf.: jam scrutari mitto,: mitte male loqui,: cetera mitte loqui,: illud dicere,: quaerere,: mitto iam de rege quaerere,: hoc exsequi mitto,: incommoda mortalium deflere,, ext. 2.— With quod: mitto, quod omnes meas tempestates subire paratissimus fueris,.—With de. mitto de amissā maximā parte exercitūs (sc. dicere), : verum, ut haec missa faciam, quae, etc.,: missos facere quaestus triennii,.—
To let go, let loose, to quit, release, dismiss: mitte rudentem, sceleste, Tr. Mittam, : unde mittuntur equi, nunc dicuntur carceres, Müll.: quadrijuges aequo carcere misit equos,; : mittin' me intro?will you let me go in?: cutem,to let go, quit,: mitte me,let me alone,: nos missos face,: missum fieri,to be let loose, set at liberty,: eum missum feci, Caes. ap. , G, 2: nec locupletare amicos umquam suos destitit, mittere in negotium,to set up in business,: sub titulum lares, to put a bill on one's house, i. e. to offer it for sale or to be let, : in consilium, to let the judges go and consult, i. e. to send the judges to make out their verdict, : sues in hostes,to set upon,: se in aliquem, to fall upon, assail, attack: vota enim faceretis, ut in eos se potius mitteret, quam in vestras possessiones, (B. and K. immitteret): se in foedera,to enter into, conclude, make,: missos faciant honores,to let go, renounce, not trouble one's self about,: vos missos facio, et quantum potest, abesse ex Africā jubeo,: missam facere legionem,to dismiss,: remotis, sive omnino missis lictoribus,: Lolliam Paulinam conjunxit sibi, brevique missam fecit,put her away,; .—
To let or bring out, to put forth, send out, emit: sanguinem incisā venā, to let blood, to bleed, : sanguinem alicui,; .—Trop.: mittere sanguinem provinciae, to bleed, i. e. drain, exhaust, ; cf.: missus est sanguis invidiae sine dolore,: radices,to put forth roots, to take root,: folium,to put forth leaves,: florem,to blossom, bloom,: membranas de corpore,to throw off, shed,: serpens horrenda sibila misit,gave forth, emitted,: mittere vocem, to utter a sound, raise one's voice, speak, say: vocem pro me ac pro re publica nemo mittit,speaks a word,: vocem liberam,to speak with freedom,: flens diu vocem non misit,: adeo res miraculo fuit, ut unus ex barbaris miserit vocem, etc.,: repente vocem sancta misit Religio,: nec labra moves, cum mittere vocem debueras,: haec Scipionis oratio ex ipsius ore Pompeii mitti videbatur,: Afranios sui timoris signa misisse,have showed signs of fear,: signa,: signum sanguinis,to show signs of blood, look bloody,.—
To send, throw, hurl, cast, launch: hastam,: pila,: lapides in aliquem,to throw,: fulmina,to hurl,: aliquid igni,: de ponte,to cast, precipitate,: praecipitem aliquem ex arce,: se saxo ab alto,to cast one's self down,: se in rapidas aquas,: se in medium,to plunge into the midst,. —Of nets: retia misit,.—Of dice, to throw: talis enim jactatis, ut quisque canem, aut senionem miserat, etc., Aug. ap. : talos in phimum,: panem alicui,to throw to,: Alexandrum manum ad arma misisse,laid his hand on his weapons,: pira in vasculo,: fert missos Vestae pura patella cibos,: accidere in mensas ut rosa missa solet,which one has let fall,.—
= πέμπειν, to attend, guide, escort: alias (animas) sub Tartara tristia mittit (Mercurius),; cf.: sic denique victor Trinacriā fines Italos mittēre relictā,.—Hence, P. a.: Missus, a, um; as subst.: Missus, i, m., he that is sent, the messenger or ambassador of God, i. e. Christ, ; .

la:noun:missus.html:
missus, ūs, m.
mitto
,
a sending away, a sending, despatching.
Lit.
missu Caesaris ad Ambiorigem ventitare consueverat, : duas venisse legiones missu Caesaris,: Archippi regis missu,: quae valido venit contorta falarica missu, Enn. ap. (Ann. v. 534 Vahl.).—
A throwing, hurling, launching: pilum, haud paulo quam hasta vehementius ictu missuque telum, Weissenb. ad loc.: telorum, Auct. B. Hisp. 17, 3; 31, 1.—
Transf.
A cast, a shot: vix absunt nobis missus bis mille sagittae,.—
In the public games, a course, a round, a heat: spectaculum multiplicatis missibus in serum produxit,; : unus est missus qui ordinarius dicitur, Schol. .—
At table, a course: novem libras carnis per tres missus ponebat,; .

la:adj:mirificus.html:
mīrĭfĭcus, a, um, adj.
mirus-facio
,
causing wonder or admiration, wonderful, marvellous, extraordinary, singular, strange (class.).
Of persons: voramus litteras cum homine mirifico ... Dionysio,: homo in doctrinis mirificus,.—
Of things: turris mirificis operibus exstructa,: pugnae,: convicium,: voluptas,: studium,: mirificas gratias agere,: sed te mirificam in latebram conjecisti,.—Sup., in two forms: mirificissimum facinus,: mirificentissima potentia, , 18, 42 init.—Hence, adv.: mīrĭfĭcē, wonderfully, marvellously, extraordinarily, exceedingly (class.): delectari,: dolere,: diligere,: laudare,: prodesse,.

la:noun:minae.html:
mĭnae, ārum, f.
root min-, only in Lat.; cf.: mentum, minari, and perh. mons
,
the projecting points or pinnacles of walls (only poet.).
Lit.: minae murorum,: moenium,; ; ; 20, 6, 2.—
Trop., threats, menaces, of animate and inanimate things (class.).
Of living beings: si quidem hercle Aeacidinis minis animisque expletus cedit,: virtutem hominibus instituendo et persuadendo, non minis et vi ac metu tradi,: terrēre minis, Enn. ap. Müll. (Ann. v. 261): minas jactare,to throw out threats,: intendere alicui,. —Of the threats used by cattle-drivers, .—Poet., of a bull: nullae in fronte minae, ; of a snake: tol lentemque minas, raising threats, i. e. raising himself in a threatening posture, .—
Of inanimate things (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): aspice, quam saevas increpat aura minas,: hibernae,: ingentes parturit ira minas,: caelestes minae territabant,; forebodings of misfortune, .

la:adj:miser.html:
mĭser, ĕra, ĕrum, adj.
prob. Sanscr. root mi-; cf. minuo; akin to Gr. μῖσος; Lat. maestus, maereo
,
wretched, unfortunate, miserable, pitiable, lamentable, etc. (cf.: infelix, calamitosus).
Of persons: nihil est tam miserabile, quam ex beato miser,: homo miser, et infortunatus,: miser atque infelix,: urgeris multis miser undique curis,: o multo miserior Dolabella, quam ille, quem tu miserrimum esse voluisti,: miser, infelix, aerumnosus,: miserrimum habere aliquem,to torment,: miserrimus Fui fugitando,have exhausted myself with running, am completely tired out,.—With gen.: miseros ambitionis,.—
Of things, afflicting, sad, wretched, melancholy: miserā ambitione laborare,: misera orbitas,: misera et calamitosa res,.—
Sick, ill, indisposed, etc.: quo morbo misera sum,suffer,: homini misero non invideo medicinam,; cf.: quid illam miseram animi excrucias?: homo animo suo miser,: miserum esse ex animo,to be wretched in mind, sick at heart,.—
Violent, excessive, extravagant: amor,: cultus miser,with regard to dress,.—
Bad, vile, poor, worthless: carmen,: remedium,.—With gen.: morum, Stat. Th. 4, 403: hominem perditum miserumque,.—
As an exclamation, inserted in the midst of a sentence: ossa atque pellis sum, misera, macritudine,: miserum! (parenthetically) i. e. what a misfortune! how sad! tum pendere poenas Cecropidae jussi (miserum!) septena quotannis Corpora, .—As subst.: mĭsĕ-rum, i, n., a wretched thing, wretchedness: bonum valetudo, miserum morbus, MSS. dub. (Madv. and B. and K. miser).—Hence, adv., in two forms.
mĭsĕrē, wretchedly, miserably; desperately, vehemently, excessively, urgently (class.): est misere scriptum, Pseudole! Ps. O miserrime, : vivere,: misere amare,: deperire,: invidere,: orare aliquid,: discedere quaerens,; cf.: misere cupis abire,: ut miserius a vobis recipiatur quam ab illo capta est,: misere miser,: misere male,.—
mĭsĕrĭter, wretchedly, lamentably, sadly (ante-class.; poet.): corrumpi, Laber. ap. : alloqui,; Enn. ap. P. (Vahl. , n. 40).

la:verb:minitor.html:
mĭnĭtor, ātus, 1 (
inf. minitarier for minitari, ; .—Act. collat. form minito, āre; v.infrafin.), v. dep. freq. [1. minor], to threaten, menace a person with any thing; constr. alicui aliquid, alicui aliquā re, with inf., with acc. and inf., and absol. (class.).
Alicui aliquid: Mihin' malum minitare?: ista horribilia minitare purpuratis tuis!; : malum alicui,: fratri mortem,: virgas securesque omnibus,.—With acc.: facito istud quod minitaris,: quin consul arma minetur,: bellum,.—With dat.: quis illest qui minitatur filio?: alicui,.—
Alicui aliquā re: huic urbi ferro ignique minitantur,; : huic urbi ferro flammāque minitans, (Klotz, ferrum flammamque): Caesari gladio,.—With abl.: qui ferro minitere, Enn. ap. Fest. s. v. ningulus, p. 177 Müll. (Ann. v. 133 Vahl.).—
With inf.: quod nunc minitare facere,.—
With acc. and inf.: cur ergo minitaris tibi te vitam esse amissurum?.—(ε) Absol.: etiam, carnufex, Minitare?: noli minitari,.—Act. collat. form mĭnĭto, āre (ante-class.): quae minitas mihi,: etiam minitas? Naev. ap. : quid minitabas te facturum,; .

la:adj:minor.html:
mĭnor, ātus, 1, v. dep. (
act. collat. form, v. mino) [minae], to jut forth, project.
Lit. (only poet.): geminique minantur In caelum scopuli,: saxa minantia caelo,.—
Transf., to threaten, menace one with any thing; constr. alicui, alicui aliquid, with abl., with acc. and inf., or with ne.
In gen. (class.).
Alicui, . —
Alicui aliquid: crucem minari alicui,.—
With abl.: coepit minari interdum ferro,. —
With acc. and inf.: ab hac minatus sese abire,: dolor se patientiam debilitaturum minatur,.—(ε) With ne: minor interminorque, nequis, etc., Fleck. —
Of inanim. things: cum domus mea ardore suo deflagrationem Urbi minabatur,: plaustra populo minantur,: illa (ornus) usque minatur, et tremefacta comam concusso vertice nutat,i. e. threatens to fall, gives signs of falling,: nil color caeli minatur, Juv 14, 294: quodcumque minabitur arcus,.—
In partic., like the Gr. ἀπειλεῖν, to promise boastfully (poet.): atqui vultus erat multa et praeclara minantis,: qui magna cum minaris, extricas nihil,.—Hence, mĭnanter, adv., threateningly, with threats, = minaciter: multa minanter agat,.

la:noun:miseria.html:
mĭsĕrĭa, ae, f.
miser
,
wretchedness, unhappy condition, misfortune, misery; affliction, distress, etc.
Lit.
(Class.) Nam invidere alii bene esse, tibi male esse, miseriast, : Proloqui Caelo atque terrae Medeaï miserias, Enn. ap. (Trag. v. 292 Vahl.): quibus servitutem meā miseriā deprecor, id. ap. (Trag. v. 173 ib.): miserias voluptate sedare,: ubi virtus est, ibi esse miseria et aerumna non potest,: in miserias incidere,: de miseriis in quibus versamur,: in miseriā esse,: oneri miseriaeque esse,.—
Trouble, fatigue, irksomeness: miseriam capere,: nimiae miseriae est,is too irksome,: nimia est miseria nimis pulchrum esse hominem,: ne (Stoici) omnia superstitiosā sollicitudine et miseriā crederent,anxiety,.—Plur.: miseriae plebis crescebant,.—
Personified: Mĭsĕrĭa, the daughter of Erebus and Nox, ; Hyg. Fab. praef.

la:verb:mitigo.html:
mītĭgo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
mitis-ago
,
to make mild, soft, or tender, make ripe or mellow; to make tame, to tame (class.).
Lit.: cum aestivā maturitate alia mitigaverit, alia torruerit, (cited ap. ): mitiget auctumnus, quod maturaverit aestas,: cibum, to make soft or tender, to soften by boiling or roasting, .—Comically: misero mihi mitigabat sandalio caput, mellowed, broke, Turp. ap. Non. l. l.: hic, qui dura sedens porrecto saxa leone Mitigat,i. e. makes soft for sitting on by spreading over them a lion's skin,: Indus agros, laetificat et mitigat,to make fruitful,: vina diluendo,: silvestres arbores,: amaritudinem frugum,to soften, mitigate,: cervicum duritias,: rabiem suum,: pilos,to thin,: animal,to tame,: valetudinem temperantia,to mitigate,.—
Trop., to make mild or gentle, to pacify, soothe, calm, assuage, appease, mitigate: animum alicujus,: te aetas mitigabit,: iras,: querimonias, Col. praef.: tristitiam ac severitatem,; cf.: acerbam severitatem condimentis humanitatis,: dolores,: labores,: aliquem pecuniā,: temporum atrocitatem,: acrimonia mitigabitur laude,: aures, to soothe with explanatory representations, : metus,: feritatem animalium,: alicui aliquem, to reconcile: Hannibalem Romanis,; cf.: vix revocanti patri mitigatus est,.—Hence, mītĭganter, adv., in a soothing manner; in order to soothe, ; ; .

la:adj:mirus.html:
mīrus, a, um, adj.
Sanscr. smi; v. miror
,
wonderful, marvellous, astonishing, extraordinary (class.): mirum et magnum facinus,: mirum me desiderium tenet urbis,: miris modis odisse aliquem,wonderfully, exceedingly,; so, miris modis, adverbially,wonderfully, strangely,; ; ; : mirum in modum conversae sunt hominum mentes,astonishingly, surprisingly,: sibi mirum videri, quid in suā Galliā populo Romano negotii esset,.—With a foll. si: minime mirum, si ista res, etc.,: quid mirum in senibus, si infirmi sunt aliquando?: mirum quam or quantum, it is wonderful how, how very, how much, i. e. extraordinarily, exceedingly: mirum quam inimicus ibat, ut ego objurgarem,: id, mirum quantum profuit ad concordiam civitatis,; so, mirum ut: mirum dictu, ut sit omnis Sarmatarum virtus velut extra ipsos,: mirum ni or nisi, it would be wonderful, I should wonder, I am very much mistaken, if not, i. e. most probably, undoubtedly, : mira sunt, nisi invitavit sese in cena plusculum,: mira sunt ni Pseudulust,; Brix ad loc.: socer, et medicus me insanire aiebant: quid sit, mira sunt,I wonder what it means, it is incomprehensible to me,: mirum ni or quin, undoubtedly, certainly: quid ploras pater? Mirum ni cantem: condemnatus sum, I wonder I don't sing, of course I ought to sing, Naev. ap. : mirum, quin ab avo ejus, aut proavo acciperem,: mirum quin te advorsus dicat,: quid mirum?what wonder?.—Comp., only ante-class.: mirior inquam tibi videor, Titin. ap. Paul. ex Müll.: quid hoc mirius? Varr. ap. .—Subst.: mīra, ōrum, n., wonders, marvels: nimia mira memoras,: septem mira,the seven wonders of the world,.—Hence, adv.: mīrē, wonderfully, marvellously, strangely, uncommonly, exceedingly (class.): puero municipia mire favent,: factus canis,: laudare,: gratus,: afficere,.—With a noun: mire opifex,: mire quam illius loci cogitatio delectat,extraordinarily, exceedingly, (al. mire quantum).

la:verb:miro.html:
mīro, āre, 1,
v. a., to wonder (ante-class. collat. form of miror): quid miras? Varr. ap. : aut ambos mira aut noli mirare de eodem,: si studium mirabis, (Com. Rel. v. 108 Rib.).—

la:noun:miles.html:
mīlĕs (MEILES, Inscr. Mur. 582; late form, milex, Gromat. Vet. p. 246, 19), ĭtis, comm.
Sanscr root mil-, to unite, combine; cf.: mille, milites, quod trium millium primo legio fiebat, ac singulae tribus Titiensium, Ramnium, Lucerum milia singula militum mittebant, Müll.
,
a soldier.
Lit.
In gen.: miles, qui locum non tenuit,: legere milites, to levy, raise, Pompei, ap. a, 3: scribere,to enlist, enroll,: deligere,: ordinare,to form into companies,: mercede conducere,to hire, take into one's pay,: dimittere,to dismiss,: miles tremulus,i. e. Priam,: miles cum die, qui prodictus sit, aberat, neque excusatus erat, infrequens dabatur,.—
In partic., of foot-soldiers, infantry, in opp. to eques: tripartito milites equitesque in expeditionem inisit,: v. eques.—Opp. to the general: miles gregarius, or miles alone, a common soldier, private: strenui militis et boni imperatoris officia simul exsequebatur,; ; volgus militum, : maritim as,a soldier in sea-service, marine,.—
Transf.
Collect., the soldiery, the army (esp. freq. in the postAug. per.), ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; et saep.—
Under the emperors, an armed servant of the emperor, court-official, Cod. Th. 11, 1, 34; .—
A chessman, pawn, in the game of chess: discolor ut recto grassetur limite miles,.—
Fem., of a woman who is in childbed for the first time: et rudis ad partūs et nova miles eram,.—Of a nymph in the train of Diana: miles erat Phoebes,.—
(Eccl. Lat.) Of a servant of God or of Christ, struggling against sin, etc.: bonus Christi,.

la:verb:misceo.gloss: to mix; to mingle; to intermingle
senses: to mix; to mingle; to intermingle
to unite; to combine; to share; to associate

la:verb:misceo.html:
miscĕo, miscŭi, mixtum (mistum is found in many MSS. and edd., but is probably a corruption of copyists, representing the weakened sound of
x in later times; v. Neue, Formenl. 2, p. 556), 2, v. a.
root mik-, mig-; Sanscr. micras, mixed; Gr. μίσγω, μίγνυμι; cf. miscellus
, to mix, mingle, to intermingle, blend (for the difference between this word and temperare, v. below, II. A.; cf. confundo).
Lit.
In gen.; with abl.: (sortes) pueri manu miscentur,: toxicum antidoto,: mella Falerno,: vina Surrentina faece Falernā,: pabula sale,: nectare aquas,.— With dat.: dulce amarumque mihi,: fletum cruori,; : inter curalium virides miscere smaragdos,: cumque meis lacrimis miscuit usque suas,. —
In partic.
To join one's self to, have carnal intercourse with one: corpus cum aliquā,.—With dat.: sic se tibi misceat,: cum aliquo misceri in Venerem,: sanguinem et genus,to intermarry,.—
To mix, prepare a drink: alteri miscere mulsum,; : Veientana mihi misces,: pocula alicui,: lurida terribiles miscent aconita novercae,; cf.: miscenda Cum Styge vina bibas, = you shall die, : nullis aconita propinquis miscuit (Orestes),.—
Miscere se, or misceri, to mingle with others, to unite, assemble: miscet (se) viris,: se partibus alicujus,: ipsa ad praetoria densae Miscentur,assemble,.—
Miscere manus or proelia, to join battle, engage (poet.): miscere manus,: proelia dura,; hence, vulnera,to inflict wounds on each other,.—
Of storms, to throw into confusion, to disturb, confound, embroil (poet.): caelum terramque,: magno misceri murmure pontum,: miscent se maria,.—Hence, of persons, to raise a great commotion, make a prodigious disturbance, to move heaven and earth: caelum ac terras,: quis caelum terris non misceat et mare caelo,; cf.: mare caelo confundere,. —
Trop.
In gen., to mix, mingle, unite, etc.: dulce amarumque una nunc misces mihi,: miscent inter sese inimicitiam agitantes, Enn. ap. (Ann. v. 275 Vahl.): animum alicujus cum suo miscere,: gravitate mixtus lepos,: misce Ergo aliquid de nostris moribus,: ex dissimillimis rebus misceri et temperari,; cf., joined with temperare,; also opp. to temperare, since miscere signifies merely to mix, but temperare to mix in due proportion: haec ita mixta fuerunt, ut temperata nullo fuerint modo,.—
In partic.
To share with, impart to another; to take part in, share in a thing (rare and perhaps not ante-Aug.): cum amico omnes curas, omnes cogitationes tuas misce,share,: se negotiis,to take part in, engage in,: administrationi,: paternae hereditati,. —
(Acc. to I. B. 5.).
To throw into confusion, to embroil, disturb (class.): om

nia infima summis paria fecit, turbavit, miscuit, : rem publicam malis concionibus,: coetus,: animorum motus dicendo,: anima, quae res humanas miscuit olim,.—

To stir up, occasion, excite, rouse: ego nova quaedam misceri et concitari mala jam pridem videbam,stirred up, devised,: seditiones,—
Misceri aliquo, to be changed into: mixtus Enipeo Taenarius deus,.

la:other:Minotaurus.html:
Mīnōtaurus, i, m., = Μινώταυρος,
a monster with the head of a bull and the body of a man, the fruit of the intercourse of Pasiphaë, the wife of Minos, with a bull.
